(1) Mn2+ ion binds to ATP in a 2:1 molar ratio, and the binding constant decreases with increasing reactant concentration, and (2) Mn2+ bound to ATP is not liberated during the course or an ATP hydrolysis by dog kidney microsome preparations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of metal ion binding to ATP and to ATPase.
the mechanism of action of the Na+-K+-dependent ATPase of dog kidney microsomal membranes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results obtained indicate that the kidney microsomes are capable of trapping Mn(2+) ions in the presence of ATP, and that the mechanism for trapping the Mn(2+) may involve the formation of a complex between Mn(2+) and ATP, and the subsequent hydrolysis of ATP to adenylic acid, with the concommitant release of inorganic phosphate and the trapping of the Mn(2+).
the kidney microsomes of the dog have a specific ATP dependent metal ion trapping system which may be of importance to the metabolism of the kidney.

the ATPase activity of dog kidney microsomal membranes is not dependent upon the presence of divalent metal ions, but that the presence of these metal ions is essential for the trapping of the metal by the membranes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of Mn(II) to ATP is not a one-to-one reaction, but a two-to-one reaction.
we have shown that divalent metals such as Mn(2+) are sequestered by kidney microsomal ATP.

the binding constants of Mn(2+)-ATP and Mn(2+)-(ADP) are markedly decreased at high concentrations of the reactants, and that dog kidney microsomal membranes contain a divalent cation sequestration system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metal ion binding properties of ATP are highly concentration-dependent and that the apparent binding constants of ATP to metal ions are much higher than previously reported in the literature.
the metal ions are bound to the microsomes and are not free to react.
